conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Today: the 'w' - like English 'v': Wasser.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Reading attempts: Wasser ... wann ... wegen.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Completely right! w = always 'v'.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: And the 'z'? Zahl, Platz.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Very good - 'ts', 'Plats'!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Und hier: ich? weich? Buch? hart?
conversation.translation: And here: ich? soft? Buch? hard?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Perfect!

lessons.description: German consonants follow a handful of steady rules. After this lesson you can attack any written German word and get its consonants right on the first try.
goals: Pronounce w, z, sch, and ß the German way.
Tell the two ch sounds apart: soft after i and e, throaty after a, o, u.
Start st- and sp- words with a built-in s: 'shtadt', 'schpielen'.
lessons.intro: German looks scary but its spelling is remarkably steady. The consonants carry a few steady rules: w is a v, z is a ts, sch is the English sh, and a word-initial st sounds like sht. The lines below are sound samples, not sentences: read them out loud and do not analyze them. With these rules you can sound out any German word - even one you have never heard.

phrases.translation: Sound sample: the German w is almost always a v-sound.
Sound sample: z and tz are both ts: 'tsahl', 'Plats'.
Sound sample: sch = sh; sp- at the start says 'shp'.
Sound sample: st- at the start says 'sht': 'shtadt'.
Sound sample: ch after i or e is a soft hissing sound.
Sound sample: ch after a, o, u is the throat 'loch' sound.
Sound sample: ss and ß are both a sharp s.

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German consonant pronunciation with me. Use ONLY the sound samples from this lesson (word lists like 'Wasser, wann, warum'), never invented sentences. Ask me to read each sample out loud, then give feedback in English on specific consonant sounds: w, z, tz, sch, sp, st, both ch sounds, and ß. Keep everything very simple at A1 level.
lessons.title: Consonants: Read Them Right

vocabulary.usage: w says 'v': 'vaser'.
sch says 'sh' in native words.
ß is just a sharp s.
au sounds like 'ow' in 'now': 'haows'.
st- at the front says 'sht': 'shtuhl'.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Now: the vowels. Listening example: 'Staat' - long.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Shtaat ... Stadt? Short?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Exactly: long - short.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: 'Nein'? Is 'ei' like 'ai'?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja: ei = 'ai'. Und ie = 'ii': Liebe, Tier.
conversation.translation: Yes: ei = 'eye'. And ie = 'ee': Liebe, Tier.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Grü-ße ... ee with rounded lips?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: That is it. Very nice. More tomorrow.

lessons.description: The vowels carry the music of German. After this lesson you can handle ei vs ie, the eu 'oy', and the umlaut dots that pull every vowel forward.
goals: Say ei like 'eye', ie like 'ee', and eu like 'oy'.
Hear the long vs short difference: Staat vs Stadt.
Pronounce ä by moving a toward e; pronounce ö and ü with rounded lips.
lessons.intro: Now the vowels. Two rules do most of the work: a doubled vowel means long (der Staat), a consonant cluster after it means short (die Stadt). Then the digraphs: ei says 'eye', ie says 'ee', eu says 'oy' - and the umlaut dots do their own thing: ä moves a toward e; for ö and ü, say the vowel with rounded lips. The lines below are sound samples: read them out loud, do not analyze.

phrases.translation: Sound sample: in native words ei says 'eye'.
Sound sample: ie = long 'ee'; ü = 'ee' with rounded lips.
Sound sample: eu = 'oy'; ö = 'e' with rounded lips.
Sound sample: doubled aa = long; consonant cluster = short.
Sound sample: the umlauts ä, ö, ü - next to the plain a.
Sound sample: long u like 'Kuchen'; short u like 'put'.
Sound sample: ie is always long 'ee'.

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German vowel sounds with me. Use ONLY the samples from this lesson (Staat/Stadt, Nein, Liebe, Tier, Kuchen, Käse, Tür, schön, grün). Ask me which vowel is long or short and how ei, ie, eu, ä, ö, ü sound. Give feedback in English. Keep everything at A1 level.
lessons.title: Vowels: Long, Short, and the Umlaut Dots

vocabulary.usage: The u runs long: 'Kuu-chen'. Compare eu = 'oy': Deutsch.
ä is an open e - like the e in 'bet'.
ei says 'eye' - 'iis'.
ü: say 'ee' with rounded lips.
o before nd often runs long.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Free today: computer, hotel, restaurant.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Cinema, taxi, music, quiz.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And family: mama, papa, grandma.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Oma - grandma.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Exactly: 'grandma' long, Oma short.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: And tomorrow? More freebies?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Yes - gladly. See you soon!

lessons.description: Thousands of German words are one mouthful away from English. Bank the free ones now: they make every later conversation start above zero.
goals: Recognize international German words you already speak.
Say each cognate correctly using the consonant and vowel rules.
Start a habit of collecting free words in every new text you meet.
lessons.intro: German shares a huge international vocabulary with English - and English borrowed words like 'Kindergarten' from German. The words below are yours for free; you only need the sound rules from the last two lessons to say them well. Recognition today, real sentences soon: articles and verbs get their own lessons.

phrases.translation: Sound samples: three words you already speak.
Sound samples: same or nearly same spelling as English.
Sound samples: Kino is 'cinema' - a free word.
Sound sample: listen for the German stress - it can differ from English.
Sound samples: family words are international; Oma is grandma.
Sound samples: order these anywhere in Germany.
Sound sample: English borrowed this word from German.

lessons.practicePrompt: Quiz me on German words I already know from English (cognates). Say an English word like 'the computer', 'the bank', 'the cinema' and have me answer with the German word, then read a new cognate out loud using the sound rules. Correct only the pronunciation; do NOT test articles or sentences yet - those come in later lessons.
lessons.title: German You Already Know: Cognates

vocabulary.usage: Almost English: kom-PUU-ter.
Stress on the last syllable: ho-TEL.
Same word, German sound: 'tank'.
French word, French sound: 'res-to-RANG'.
Same spelling as English bank - the money kind too.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Hallo! Ich heiße Lena. Wie heißt du?
conversation.translation: Hello! My name is Lena. What is your name?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich heiße Jonas. Und der Hund?
conversation.translation: My name is Jonas. And the dog?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: The dog's name is Bruno.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: And Monday, Saturday?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Always 'der': Monday, Saturday.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Der Tisch, der Hund, der Montag - alles 'der'!
conversation.translation: The table, the dog, Monday - all 'der'!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Deutsch: Wort für Wort, Schritt für Schritt.
conversation.translation: German: word by word, step by step.

lessons.description: Many everyday nouns are masculine der - days and weekdays certainly are. With them you learn heißen, 'to be called': the verb of every German introduction.
goals: Say der with common masculine nouns.
Use the fixed name phrases: 'Wie heißt du?' - 'Ich heiße ...'.
Know that days of the week always take der.
lessons.intro: Every German noun wears an article, and the masculine one is der. Plenty of daily words are der: der Tisch, der Hund, der Mann - and all days of the week: der Montag. Your first verb is heißen, 'to be called'. 'Wie heißt du?' is one fixed phrase: learn it whole the way you learned 'Hallo'; the grammar of questions comes later.

phrases.translation: What is your name? (a fixed phrase - memorize it whole.)

phrases.text: Der Tisch, der Hund, der Mann.
phrases.translation: The table, the dog, the man. (all der)
Monday, Saturday. (days of the week are der)
The chair - broken. (fragment answers are fine in speech)

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German masculine nouns and the name phrases with me. Say simple objects in English and ask me to answer with der + the German noun. Then rehearse the fixed exchange 'Wie heißt du?' - 'Ich heiße ...' without breaking it into parts. Correct only the article gender and the heißen forms.
lessons.title: Masculine Nouns: der and Your First Verb

vocabulary.usage: Masculine - always learn the article with the noun.
Many animal names are der - learn each noun with its article.
People match nature: der Mann.
Days of the week are der: der Montag, der Samstag.
Ich heiße, du heißt - your first verb. The 'he is called' form arrives with pronouns in Lesson 7.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Now: 'die'. The lamp, the cat.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: The cat? And the flower?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Also 'die'. The flower is called 'Rose'.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Newspaper? Die Zeitung!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Ending '-ung'? Always 'die'.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Ending '-heit'? Die Freiheit!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Very good! '-ung', '-heit': safely 'die'.

lessons.description: The feminine family comes with a gift: two word endings make gender certain. Words in -ung and -heit are always die - a rule you will use every single day.
goals: Say die with common feminine nouns.
Trust -ung and -heit: words with those endings are always die.
Notice nature's own articles: die Sonne, der Mond.
lessons.intro: The feminine article is die, and German makes it unusually predictable: every word ending in -ung is die (die Zeitung), every word ending in -heit is die (die Freiheit). Collect the common die nouns on top of that: die Lampe, die Katze, die Sonne. Endings are German's quiet superpower - use them.

phrases.text: Die Lampe - an. Die Lampe - aus.
phrases.translation: The lamp - on. The lamp - off. (verbless: perfectly normal German)
The sun, the moon. (nature takes its own article)

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German feminine nouns with me. Say English nouns - some plain (lamp, cat) and some whose German form ends in -ung or -heit (newspaper, freedom) - and ask me to answer with die + the German noun. Ask me why those endings are safe. Correct only the article and the ending rule.
lessons.title: Feminine Nouns: die

vocabulary.usage: Words ending in -ung are always die.
Words ending in -heit are always die.
A common household die-word.
Many animal names are die - learn the article with each noun.
Nature is not logical: die Sonne, but der Mond.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und jetzt: 'das'. Das Buch, das Fenster.
conversation.translation: And now: 'das'. The book, the window.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: And Anna? 'Das Mädchen'?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Grammar, not logic: '-chen'? Always 'das'.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Das Mädchen ... das Kind ... das Buch ...
conversation.translation: The girl ... the child ... the book ...

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Genau. Und die Welt? Der Mond, die Sonne.
conversation.translation: Exactly. And the world? The moon, the sun.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Der Mond? Der. Die Sonne? Die. Das Kind? Das.
conversation.translation: The moon? Der. The sun? Die. The child? Das.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Perfect: der, die, das - complete!

lessons.description: The das family has its own guaranteed rule: every word in -chen is das. Finish the article trio here - from now on, every noun you meet can wear the right hat.
goals: Say das with common neuter nouns.
Apply the -chen rule: every diminutive is das.
Keep all three article families apart: der, die, das.
lessons.intro: Neuter is das: das Buch, das Fenster, das Kind. The famous rule is the little -chen: words in -chen are always das - even das Mädchen, the girl, because grammar is not logic. Many international words take das too: das Handy. With der, die, das behind you, learn each noun with its article from today on and every later lesson stays easier.

phrases.translation: The book - new. (verbless fragment: normal German)
Anna? 'The girl' is das - grammar over nature.
The cell phone - new. (many international words take das)

phrases.text: Der Mond, die Sonne, das Kind.
phrases.translation: The moon, the sun, the child. (each noun, its own article)

lessons.practicePrompt: Quiz me on German gender. Give me an English noun - sometimes one whose German form ends in -chen (girl), sometimes -ung or -heit (newspaper, freedom), sometimes plain - and ask me for the article and the rule behind it. Correct only the article choice and the ending rules.
lessons.title: Neuter Nouns: das, and Gender by Ending

vocabulary.usage: A core neuter noun: das Buch.
Words ending in -chen are always das - even this one.
Neuter: das Kind.
Neuter house word: das Fenster.
Many international words take das. German for 'cell phone'.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Hello - I am Lena.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Jonas. I am new here.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Ms. Keller - she is a teacher.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: And the man? A student?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: He is a student. Like us.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: And tired...

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Er ist müde. Und ich bin müde. Und du?
conversation.translation: He is tired. And I am tired. And you?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Naturally. Tired.

lessons.description: ich, du, er, sie, es - the smallest words with the biggest job. The German twist: er/sie/es follow the noun's article, not nature.
goals: Use ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr and sie (they).
Choose er/sie/es by the noun's article, not by its sex.
Use the frame 'Er/Sie/Es ist ...' and the fixed phrase 'Ich bin ...'.
lessons.intro: You know der, die, das - now they do double duty. When you point back at a noun, the pronoun copies its grammatical gender: der Tisch becomes er, die Katze becomes sie, das Kind becomes es. For people, nature usually agrees: er for a man, sie for a woman. The whole pronoun map is ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie. Everything today rides on one fixed frame, 'Er ist nett' - the full verb parade happens in the next lesson.

phrases.translation: I am Jonas. (one fixed phrase today - the full drill is Lesson 8.)
He is nice. (also 'it is nice' when the noun is der.)
She is a teacher. (also 'it is' for a die-noun.)
It is cold. (es without any noun behind it.)
The table? It is old. (er follows der.)
The cat? It is black. (sie follows die.)
The child? It is small. (es follows das.)
Mr. Weiß? He is a university student.
we, you all, they - the full set. (the matching verb forms come in Lesson 8)

lessons.practicePrompt: Play a meeting-new-people game with me: point at people and things using noun chunks with their article (der Hund, die Lampe, das Kind) and have me answer with the fixed frame 'Er/Sie/Es ist ...' or the memorized 'Ich bin ...'. Do not use question words yet - they are Lesson 14. Correct only the pronoun choice, especially er/sie/es for objects.
lessons.title: Who Is Who: Personal Pronouns

vocabulary.usage: Frau Keller = Ms. Keller; also 'the woman'.
Masculine; the female form is die Studentin.
Professions add -in for the female form.
Er ist nett. Sie ist nett. A word you will use daily.
Ich bin müde. Er ist müde. Guess how the class ends.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Practice: the verb 'sein'. I ...?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: I am!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: You ...?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: You are!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: He, she, it ...?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Er ist, sie ist, es ist. Und zusammen? Wir sind!
conversation.translation: He is, she is, it is. And together? We are!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und die Frage: Bist du bereit?
conversation.translation: And the question: Are you ready?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich bin bereit. Und müde. Das bin ich immer!
conversation.translation: I am ready. And tired. That is me, always!

lessons.description: sein - to be - is the most-used verb in German, and completely irregular. Its six shapes are the first poem of the course: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind.
goals: Conjugate sein for all six persons.
Flip sein into questions: Bist du ...? Seid ihr ...?
Use the pointer das: 'Das ist der Tisch' - 'Das bin ich'.
lessons.intro: German's engine is sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind. No trick makes it regular, so drill it like a poem - you just met its 'ist' form in the last lesson. Questions are only a word-order flip: Bist du bereit? And das is the universal pointer: Das ist der Tisch, das bin ich. After this lesson you can say who everyone and everything is.

phrases.translation: They are ready. (small sie, many people)
That is the table. (das, the pointer)
That is me. (point at a photo)

lessons.practicePrompt: Drill the verb sein with me: call out a subject (ich, du, der Hund, wir, ihr, sie alle) and ask me for the right sein form; then flip statements into questions (Bist du ...? Seid ihr ...?) and use the pointer das ('Das ist der Tisch', 'Das bin ich'). Correct only sein forms and the question flip.
lessons.title: Being Everything: the Verb sein

vocabulary.usage: Ich bin, du bist, er ist - irregular; drill it like a poem.
Bist du bereit? Seid ihr bereit?
Ich bin fertig! - I am done!
Alle müde? Ja, alle.
Wir sind hier. - We are here.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: This one here: the lamp.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: This lamp is beautiful.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And the chair? This one...?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Dieser Stuhl ist neu. Nicht alt.
conversation.translation: This chair is new. Not old.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And this word? 'new'?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Dieses Wort: 'neu'. Der Stuhl ist neu.
conversation.translation: This word: 'new'. The chair is new.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Exactly: dieser, diese, dieses.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Und das Buch? Dieses Buch ist super.
conversation.translation: And the book? This book is great.

lessons.description: Point like a German: dieser, diese, dieses copy the article of whatever you point at. Three words, and every object near you becomes conversation.
goals: Match dieser/diese/dieses to the noun's article.
Contrast plain der ('the') with dieser ('this one').
Point with short statements: 'Dieser Stuhl ist neu'.
lessons.intro: You already point with 'Das ist der Tisch'. The upgrade is dieser - 'this one' - and it just borrows the article you already know: dieser for der-words, diese for die-words, dieses for das-words. That is the whole lesson. Look around the room: every table, lamp and book is now a sentence waiting to happen.

phrases.text: Der Stuhl? Dieser Stuhl ist neu.
phrases.translation: The chair? This chair is new. (der = the, dieser = this one)
The word? This word is called 'old'.

lessons.practicePrompt: Play a pointing game with me: name an object with its article (der Stuhl, die Lampe, das Buch) and have me say a short statement 'Dieser/Diese/Dieses + noun + ist + adjective'. Keep every adjective after the verb - never an adjective directly before a noun. Correct only the dieser/diese/dieses choice.
lessons.title: This One, That One: dieser, diese, dieses

vocabulary.usage: der → dieser, die → diese, das → dieses.
Masculine: dieser Kurs.
Neuter: dieses Wort. A word worth knowing.
Ending -ung - you know the rule: die Übung.
Very common in spoken German - yes, like English.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Hast du eine Minute? Ich habe eine Frage.
conversation.translation: Do you have a minute? I have a question.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ja, ich habe Zeit. Was ist los?
conversation.translation: Yes, I have time. What is up?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich habe mein Buch nicht. Es ist weg!
conversation.translation: I do not have my book. It is gone!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Your book is here!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: True! Thanks, Jonas.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: No problem.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Dann sind wir fertig. Jetzt: Kaffee!
conversation.translation: Then we are done. Now: coffee!

lessons.description: German's second power verb plus its friendliest little words: a, no, my, your. One pattern to learn and five words to master.
goals: Conjugate haben and use it in daily sentences.
Use ein and kein to say you have something or you do not.
Say what is yours with mein and dein.
lessons.intro: haben (to have) is the verb you need most when talking about your life: ich habe, du hast, er hat. It is irregular - the b disappears in du hast and er hat - so drill it early. The words ein (a), kein (no), mein (my) and dein (your) all behave exactly like ein, so learning one pattern gives you four words for free.

phrases.translation: We are hungry (literally: we have hunger).

lessons.practicePrompt: Play my roommate: we are looking for things around the flat. Ask me what I have and what I am looking for. I should use haben, ein, kein, mein and dein with the right forms. Correct only those words.
lessons.title: Having Things: haben and ein, kein, mein, dein

vocabulary.usage: ich habe, du hast, er hat - the b disappears in du hast and er hat.
Uncountable and singular: 'Ich habe kein Geld.'
Feminine: die Tasche.
Masculine 'a' will change after verbs: ein Mann -> einen Mann (case lesson 7).
Negates a noun: kein Geld, keine Zeit.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: What are you doing here?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich lerne Deutsch. Und du? Arbeitest du hier?
conversation.translation: I learn German. And you? Do you work here?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja, ich arbeite schon lange hier.
conversation.translation: Yes, I have been working here a long time. (literally: I work here already long)

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich wohne auch hier. Meine Schwester wohnt auch hier.
conversation.translation: I live here too. My sister lives here too.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: What are you doing this evening?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Heute Abend bleibe ich zu Hause. Morgen komme ich wieder.
conversation.translation: This evening I stay at home. Tomorrow I come back.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Dann bis morgen! Viel Spaß zu Hause!
conversation.translation: See you tomorrow then! Enjoy your evening at home!

lessons.description: The German engine: verb endings -e, -st, -t, -en and the law that the verb is always second.
goals: Conjugate regular verbs in the present tense.
Keep the verb in second position, even after time words.
Form yes/no questions and w-questions in the present.
lessons.intro: Regular German verbs are almost mechanical: ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen. The endings are -e, -st, -t, -en - only the du and er/sie/es forms really need memory. The bigger rule is about position: the verb is always the second element of the sentence. Start with 'Morgen' and the subject flips behind the verb: Morgen lerne ich.

phrases.translation: Tomorrow I stay at home. (verb still second!)

phrases.text: Heute lernen wir, morgen arbeiten wir.
phrases.translation: Today we learn, tomorrow we work.

lessons.practicePrompt: Chat with me about our daily routines in German. Ask me simple questions with was, wo and wann. Correct only the verb endings and the verb-second word order.
lessons.title: Present Tense: regular verbs and word order

vocabulary.usage: Regular model verb: ich lerne, du lernst.
Adds an extra e: er arbeitet (not 'er arb-tet').
Regular: du spielst, er spielt.
'Ich wohne in Berlin.'
'Ich bleibe zu Hause.'

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: What are you doing Saturday?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: I am going to Berlin!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Nach Berlin? Wie lang fährst du?
conversation.translation: To Berlin? How long are you traveling?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Nicht lange. Und du? Was machst du?
conversation.translation: Not long. And you? What are you doing?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich arbeite und lese wie immer.
conversation.translation: I work and read as always.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Du arbeitest viel. Wirst du nicht müde?
conversation.translation: You work a lot. Are you not getting tired?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja. Ich werde müde - gute Nacht!
conversation.translation: Yes. I am getting tired - good night!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Good night! See you Monday!

lessons.description: The most common verbs break the pattern for du and er: du fährst, er spricht, sie liest, du isst. Plus werden: the verb of change.
goals: Use vowel-changing verbs correctly after du and er/sie/es.
Conjugate werden and use it for changes.
Talk about routines, food and weather with these verbs.
lessons.intro: A handful of very common verbs change their vowel in du and er/sie/es forms: a becomes ä (du fährst), e becomes i (du sprichst), e becomes ie (er liest). The ich and wir forms stay normal, so you only learn the breaking forms once each. Then come meet werden (to become): the verb for everything that changes - weather, mood, plans.

phrases.translation: I am going home. (fahren: du fährst)
He speaks three languages. (sprechen: du sprichst)
She is reading a book. (lesen: er liest)
What do you like to read?
You sleep too much. (schlafen: du schläfst)
What are you eating? (essen: du isst)

lessons.practicePrompt: Talk with me in German about our weekend and about food. Make me use the vowel-changing verbs fahren, sprechen, lesen, essen, schlafen after du and er. Correct only those forms and werden forms.
lessons.title: Vowel-Changing Verbs and werden

vocabulary.usage: e becomes i: du sprichst, er spricht.
a becomes ä: du fährst, er fährt.
e becomes ie: du liest, er liest.
e becomes i and doubles: du isst, er isst.
du wirst, er wird - and later it builds the passive voice.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: What are you looking for?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: I am looking for my key.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Die Tür ist offen. Du brauchst den Schlüssel nicht!
conversation.translation: The door is open. You do not need the key!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Stimmt! Ich sehe den Schlüssel. Da ist er!
conversation.translation: True! I see the key. There it is!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Du suchst den Schlüssel jeden Tag!
conversation.translation: You look for the key every day!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Sehr lustig. Ich hole den Kaffee - ohne Zucker für dich?
conversation.translation: Very funny. I am getting the coffee - without sugar for you?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: For me with sugar, please!

lessons.description: German marks the thing you do something to: ich sehe den Mann, ich habe einen Hund. Only masculine shouts about it.
goals: Use den/einen/meinen after verbs with masculine nouns.
Use the pronouns mich and dich.
Build phrases with für, ohne and gegen.
lessons.intro: When an action hits an object, that object is in the accusative. Only one gender advertises this: masculine. der becomes den, ein becomes einen, mein becomes meinen. Feminine, neuter and plural look identical to the nominative, so you only fight one gender. Prepositions für, ohne and gegen also always put their word in the accusative.

phrases.translation: Are you looking for your key?
I see the man over there.
I will pick you up later.

lessons.practicePrompt: Play hide-and-seek objects with me in German. Name things we lose, need or buy, and make me say them in the accusative after verbs like sehen, brauchen, suchen, nehmen, kaufen. Correct only the masculine accusative forms (den, einen, meinen, dich, mich).
lessons.title: The Accusative: what the action hits

vocabulary.usage: der Mann -> Ich sehe den Mann.
Ich habe einen Bruder.
The object form of ich: 'Er kennt mich.'
The object form of du: 'Ich hole dich.'
Takes the accusative: 'Ich brauche deinen Rat.'

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Why are you laughing?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich denke an gestern. Mein Bruder fragte: 'Wann kommst du?' Und ich sagte: 'Morgen.'
conversation.translation: I am thinking about yesterday. My brother asked: 'When are you coming?' And I said: 'Tomorrow.'

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And are you coming tomorrow?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ja. Dann lernen wir zusammen. Gut?
conversation.translation: Yes. Then we study together. Good?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Sehr gern. Früher lernte ich oft allein.
conversation.translation: With pleasure. Earlier I often studied alone.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Allein? Morgen lernen wir zusammen. Das ist besser!
conversation.translation: Alone? Tomorrow we study together. That is better!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja! Morgen lesen wir ein Buch.
conversation.translation: Yes! Tomorrow we read a book.

lessons.description: Tell what happened with the simple written past of regular verbs, and learn to ask with w-words: was, wer, wo, wann, warum, wie.
goals: Form the -te past of regular verbs.
Use past time words like gestern and früher.
Ask open questions with all six w-words.
lessons.intro: German storytelling has a compact past for regular verbs: add -te. ich lernte, du lerntest, er lernte, wir lernten. You will hear it in books, news and fairy tales - and it is the fastest way to sound like you read German. To learn anything you must also ask about it, so this lesson brings the w-words too: was, wer, wo, wann, warum, wie.
lessons.practicePrompt: Talk with me in German about yesterday and about plans. Ask me questions with was, wer, wo, wann, warum and wie, and let me answer in the -te past of regular verbs. Correct only the -te forms and the w-question words.
lessons.title: Telling Stories: the -te past and real questions
lessons.topic: Simple past of regular verbs and question words

vocabulary.usage: A common word in past sentences: 'Gestern lernte ich ...'
'Früher wohnte ich in Köln.'
Ask for reasons: 'Warum lachst du?'
Past: er sagte.
Past: sie fragte. A verb built for questions.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: How many brothers do you have?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Zwei. Tom ist dreißig und Ben ist achtundzwanzig.
conversation.translation: Two. Tom is thirty and Ben is twenty-eight.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: What do you like to do together?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Wir sehen gern Filme - gestern auch! Ben war hier.
conversation.translation: We like watching films - yesterday too! Ben was here.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und der Film gestern? War er gut?
conversation.translation: And the film? Was it good?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich war begeistert. Ben war müde und ging sofort nach Hause!
conversation.translation: I was thrilled. Ben was tired and went straight home!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Typical family!

lessons.description: The five irregular past forms you will use every day, plus numbers and plurals so you can talk about your own life.
goals: Use war, hatte, ging, kam and sah naturally.
Say your age and understand numbers up to 100.
Form the most common plurals (-e, -er, -s).
lessons.intro: The most important verbs refuse to follow the regular past pattern: sein becomes war, haben becomes hatte, gehen becomes ging, kommen becomes kam, sehen becomes sah. There is no trick - just memorize these five and you can tell stories about yesterday, your age and your family. Numbers count too: German says the tens after the units, so 28 is achtundzwanzig.

phrases.translation: How many books do you have?

phrases.text: Ich habe zwei Brüder und eine Schwester.
phrases.translation: I have two brothers and one sister.

lessons.practicePrompt: Interview me in German about my life and my yesterday: my age, my family, what I was and what I had. Make me use war, hatte, ging, kam, sah and real numbers. Correct only the irregular past forms and the numbers.
lessons.title: Story Past: war, hatte, ging, kam

vocabulary.usage: ich war, du warst, er war.
ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte.
German flips numbers: 26 = sechsundzwanzig (six-and-twenty).
A common plural: add -er and an umlaut.
Neuter nouns often take -er plus umlaut in the plural.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich verstehe das nicht. Hilfst du mir?
conversation.translation: I do not understand this. Will you help me?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Of course. What do you not understand?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Der ganze Dativ! Meine Schwester sagte: Die Übungen gefallen dir bald.
conversation.translation: The whole dative! My sister said: you will like the exercises soon.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Sie hat recht. Ich fahre jetzt mit dem Bus. Morgen erkläre ich dir alles!
conversation.translation: She is right. I am going by bus now. Tomorrow I will explain everything to you!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und danach? Trinken wir einen Kaffee?
conversation.translation: And after that? Shall we drink a coffee?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Gern. Nach dem Kurs schmeckt der Kaffee besser.
conversation.translation: Gladly. After the course the coffee tastes better.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: You explain well - see you tomorrow!

lessons.description: The case for everything that arrives at someone: ich helfe dir, das Buch gehört mir, der Kurs gefällt mir.
goals: Use dem, der and den + n after dative verbs and prepositions.
Use the pronouns mir and dir.
Say what you like with gefallen.
lessons.intro: The dative is the receiver case: you help someone, something belongs to someone, something pleases someone - though some verbs and prepositions simply demand it. Masculine and neuter take dem, feminine becomes der; in the plural the article is den and the noun usually gains -n too (mit den Kindern). A handful of verbs (helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken) and prepositions (mit, zu, nach, aus, von) demand the dative automatically, so you learn them together with the case.

phrases.translation: I help you. (natural English: I'll help you)
I like the course. (literally: the course pleases me)
We are going to the train station. (zum = zu + dem)

phrases.text: Nach dem Kurs trinke ich Kaffee.
phrases.translation: After the course I will drink coffee.

phrases.text: Das Geschenk ist von meiner Schwester.
phrases.translation: The gift is from my sister.
How are you? (literally: how goes it to you)

lessons.practicePrompt: Role-play everyday situations with me (station, cafe, classroom) where I must offer help, talk about what I like and what belongs to me. Make me use dative articles and mir/dir. Correct only the dative forms.
lessons.title: The Dative: giving, helping, liking

vocabulary.usage: Always + dative: 'Ich helfe dir.'
'Das gefällt mir.' - I like it.
Always + dative: 'Das gehört mir.'
Always + dative: 'mit dem Bus', 'mit der Bahn'.
'zum Bahnhof' = zu + dem; 'zur Arbeit' = zu + der.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Was willst du nach dem Kurs machen?
conversation.translation: What do you want to do after the course?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich will nur Kaffee trinken. Und du?
conversation.translation: I just want to drink coffee. And you?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich muss arbeiten, aber ich kann später kommen.
conversation.translation: I have to work, but I can come later.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Dann trinken wir um acht. Kennst du ein gutes Café?
conversation.translation: Then let us drink at eight. Do you know a good cafe?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja! Die Eule ist klein, aber der Kaffee ist super.
conversation.translation: Yes! The Eule is small, but the coffee is great.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Do we have to reserve?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Nein, kein Problem. Dann treffen wir uns um acht Uhr.
conversation.translation: No, no problem. Then we meet at eight o'clock.

lessons.description: Say what you can, must and want to do - with the second verb at the end - and connect ideas with und, aber, oder, denn.
goals: Conjugate können, müssen and wollen.
Send the second verb to the end of the sentence.
Connect sentences with und, aber, oder and denn.
lessons.intro: Modal verbs color the action: ich kann (ability), ich muss (necessity), ich will (intention). Two golden rules: ich and er look identical (ich kann, er kann - no ending), and the real action goes to the very end as an infinitive. Then conjunctions: und, aber, oder and denn keep the normal word order, so they are free to use today.

phrases.translation: Do we have to pay today?
What do you want to do?

phrases.text: Wir können kommen, aber Tom kann nicht.
phrases.translation: We can come, but Tom cannot.

phrases.text: Ich trinke keinen Kaffee, sondern Tee.
phrases.translation: I do not drink coffee, but tea instead. (sondern corrects a negation)

phrases.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, denn ich will in Berlin arbeiten.
phrases.translation: I am learning German because I want to work in Berlin.

phrases.text: Du musst nicht suchen - ich habe den Schlüssel!
phrases.translation: You do not have to search - I have the key!

lessons.practicePrompt: Give me short situations in German (exam tomorrow, no money, cannot sleep) and let me answer with können, müssen or wollen plus a verb at the end. Also let me connect two ideas with und, aber, oder, denn. Correct only the modal forms and the verb-at-the-end rule.
lessons.title: Modal Verbs: können, müssen, wollen

vocabulary.usage: ich kann, du kannst, er kann.
ich muss, du musst, er muss - no ending in ich/er.
ich will, du willst, er will.
A conjunction that does not change word order.
Like und and aber, denn keeps normal verb-second order: 'Ich lerne Deutsch, denn ich will in Berlin arbeiten.'
After a no: 'Ich trinke keinen Kaffee, sondern Tee.'

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: What did you do yesterday?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich habe den ganzen Tag gelernt.
conversation.translation: I studied the whole day.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Nur das? Aber gestern war das Wetter schön!
conversation.translation: Only that? But yesterday the weather was nice!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich weiß. Ich war im Büro und habe den ganzen Tag gelernt.
conversation.translation: I know. I was in the office and studied the whole day.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And now?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Jetzt habe ich frei. Ich habe einen Kuchen gekauft!
conversation.translation: Now I am off. I bought a cake!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: A cake? What is going on?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich habe heute viel gelernt - jetzt habe ich gute Laune!
conversation.translation: I studied a lot today - now I am in a good mood!

lessons.description: The past tense Germans actually use when they talk: haben plus a ge- word at the end of the sentence.
goals: Form regular past participles (ge- ... -t).
Put haben in second position and the participle at the end.
Know when war and hatte are better than a participle.
lessons.intro: In much spoken German, completed actions take the present perfect: ich habe gekauft, du hast gelernt, wir haben gemacht - haben in position two, the ge- word at the very end. Regular ge- words are mechanical: ge + stem + t. The written past (lernte) survives mainly in books and news, and in conversation war, hatte, konnte and musste stay short and common.

phrases.text: Sie hat den ganzen Tag gearbeitet.
Der Kurs hat eine Stunde gedauert.
Ich habe die Frage nicht gehört.
phrases.translation: I did not hear the question.

phrases.text: Gestern war ich müde, deshalb habe ich nichts gemacht.
phrases.translation: Yesterday I was tired, so I did not do anything.

lessons.practicePrompt: Ask me in German about yesterday, last weekend and last summer. Make me answer in the spoken past: ich habe ... gemacht, gelernt, gekauft. Correct only the participle form and the have-verb position, and remind me when war or hatte is the right choice.
lessons.title: The Spoken Past: ich habe Kaffee gekauft

vocabulary.usage: Regular participle: ge + mach + t.
ge + lern + t.
ge + such + t.
sagen becomes gesagt (no umlaut, no surprise).
Verbs with be- prefix skip the ge-: bezahlen -> bezahlt.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: When do you usually get up?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich wache um sechs auf, aber ich stehe erst um sieben auf.
conversation.translation: I wake up at six, but I only get up at seven.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Früh! Ich brauche zuerst meinen Kaffee.
conversation.translation: Early! I need my coffee first.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich kaufe ein frisches Brot, und du machst den Kaffee?
conversation.translation: I am buying a fresh loaf of bread, and you make the coffee?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Abgemacht. Bringst du auch Äpfel mit?
conversation.translation: Deal. Will you bring apples too?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Die alten Äpfel sind noch gut!
conversation.translation: The old apples are still good!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Dann bringen wir keine Äpfel mit.
conversation.translation: Then we are not bringing any apples.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Gut. Der Kurs fängt gleich an!
conversation.translation: Good. The course starts soon!

lessons.description: Say a good story in German, not just a story: ein großes Brot, eine neue Tasche. And learn verbs that split themselves in two.
goals: Add the right ending to adjectives before a noun.
Use separable verbs with the prefix at the end.
Recognize common prefixes: auf-, ein-, an-, mit-, fern-.
lessons.intro: Two final upgrades make you sound fluent. Adjectives before a noun wear endings - the tiny cousin of the article sits on the adjective: ein gutes Brot, eine neue Tasche, einen heißen Kaffee. And separable verbs split: the prefix escapes to the end of the sentence. Ich stehe um sieben auf. Wir kaufen am Samstag ein. Both are pure pattern.

phrases.translation: I am drinking a hot coffee.
She is buying a new bag.

phrases.text: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
phrases.translation: I get up at seven o'clock.
We do the grocery shopping on Saturdays.

phrases.text: Der Kurs fängt um acht an.
phrases.translation: The course starts at eight. (anfangen: fängt ... an)

lessons.practicePrompt: Describe daily-life objects and routines with me in German: my room, my breakfast, my morning. Make me use adjective endings before nouns and separable verbs like aufstehen, einkaufen, anfangen, mitbringen. Correct only adjective endings and prefix placement.
lessons.title: Rich Descriptions: adjective endings and separable verbs

vocabulary.usage: Separable: 'Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf.'
'Wir kaufen ein.'
'Der Film fängt an.' - and note the a becomes ä.
'Ich sehe fern.' - even stronger: 'du siehst fern.'
'Bringst du Kuchen mit?'

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Erzähl mir von dir! Wo bist du geboren?
conversation.translation: Tell me about yourself! Where were you born?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: I was born in 1994 in Krakow.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und wann bist du nach Deutschland gekommen?
conversation.translation: And when did you come to Germany?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Letztes Jahr im Mai. Ich bin mit dem Zug gefahren.
conversation.translation: Last year in May. I travelled by train.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und der erste Tag? Was hast du gemacht?
conversation.translation: And the first day? What did you do?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich bin viel gelaufen und ich habe Pizza gegessen. Ich war müde, aber glücklich.
conversation.translation: I walked a lot and I ate pizza. I was tired, but happy.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And what is your goal?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich will gut Deutsch sprechen. Ich lerne jeden Tag!
conversation.translation: I want to speak German well. I learn every day!

lessons.description: The final piece: the ge- words that change (gegessen, gefahren), the verbs that take sein, and dates and times - so you can finally tell your story in the German past.
goals: Use the most common irregular past participles.
Choose sein or haben correctly in the spoken past.
Say birth years, dates and clock time.
lessons.intro: Common verbs keep a vowel change in their ge- word: essen - gegessen, sprechen - gesprochen, fahren - gefahren. And many intransitive verbs describing a change of location or state take sein, not haben: ich bin gefahren, ich bin gekommen, ich bin geblieben. Learn the helper together with the verb. Add dates - ich bin 1994 geboren, halb neun, im Mai - and you can finally tell your whole story in German.

phrases.text: Bist du mit dem Zug gefahren?
Mein Geburtstag ist am ersten Mai.
phrases.translation: My birthday is on May the first. (am + ordinal number for exact dates)
My grandpa died in 2010. (sterben takes sein: ist gestorben)
It is 8:30. (German counts toward the next hour)
I stayed at home. (bleiben takes sein)
I slept for a long time. (schlafen takes haben)
I moved to Berlin. (in the sense of relocating home, umziehen takes sein)

lessons.practicePrompt: Interview me about my life story in German: when and where I was born, when I came to this city, what I did last year, what I ate and drank. Make me choose between sein and haben and use irregular participles. Also ask my birthday and what time it is, and make me say one date with an ordinal number (am ersten Mai). Correct only the perfect tense helper, the participle form, and dates.
lessons.title: Your Story: irregular participles, sein-perfect and dates

vocabulary.usage: haben + gegessen: 'Wir haben gegessen.'
sein + gefahren: 'Ich bin gefahren.'
Always sein: 'Ich bin gekommen.'
'Ich bin 1995 geboren.' Dates in German: day.month.year - 05.10.1999.
laufen takes sein: 'Ich bin viel gelaufen.'
Dates use ordinals: der erste, der zweite, der zehnte - 'am ersten Mai'.
